title: Locking transition in coupled disordered systems
abstract: When a system of many interacting constituents is extended across space, every region carries the same disordered landscape, and it is unclear whether distant regions settle into the same state. We study copies of the Random Energy Model (REM), sharing one disorder realization, coupled along a chain. A first-order transition separates a phase with short-range correlations, from a locked phase in which the entire chain occupies the lowest-energy state with probability one, even at positive temperature. No intermediate ordering lengths occur. In the Generalized REM the chain locks either to the lowest-energy state or to the lowest free-energy valley.
summary: This work analyzes the locking transition in coupled disordered systems modeled by the Random Energy Model. It establishes that the transition between correlated and fully locked phases is first-order, depending critically on the nature of the coupling. The findings provide detailed theoretical insights into how disorder dictates macroscopic phase behavior in extended quantum or classical systems.
main_problem: The paper investigates the locking transition in coupled disordered systems, specifically determining if the entire chain settles into the lowest-energy state with probability one at positive temperature.
main_result: The transition between the short-range correlated phase and the locked phase is found to be first-order, and the system can exhibit complex locking behavior depending on the coupling structure (e.g., locking to the lowest free-energy valley).
method: The analysis uses techniques from statistical mechanics, including calculating free energy densities, saddle-point approximations, and analyzing domain factorizations for large chain lengths.
model_or_system: The model consists of copies of the Random Energy Model (REM) coupled along a one-dimensional chain, generalized to the GREM. The Hamiltonian involves coupling terms ($\psi$) between neighboring copies.
key_observables: Free energy density ($f$), transition temperature ($T^*$), domain lengths ($L$), and the overlap parameter ($\alpha$).
important_parameters: Temperature ($T$), coupling strength ($\epsilon$), chain length ($L$), and system size ($N$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the thermodynamic limit ($L 	o \infty, N 	o \infty$) and uses approximations like domain factorization and saddle-point methods.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the phase diagram showing the transition between free and locked phases for different coupling types, and show the free energy density $g(T, \epsilon)(x)$ dependence on domain size.
paper_structure: The paper systematically analyzes the free energy landscape by comparing different coupling structures (state-matched vs. structured) and generalizing the model to the GREM, establishing the conditions for the three possible phases.
why_interesting: The study of glassy dynamics and phase transitions in disordered systems, particularly those involving energy landscapes and domain formation, provides theoretical tools applicable to understanding complex quantum many-body systems far from equilibrium.
